name: Eastern Uzh Romani, a North Central Romani variety
confidence_why: Beníšek 2017, a first-hand grammar of Eastern Uzh Romani, gives fixed penultimate stress with worked examples and states that this is a contact feature of all Eastern North Central dialects, and the one dissenting description, von Sowa 1887 on the West Slovak Romani of Trenčín where Slovak initial stress had nearly displaced the penultimate rule, concerns a different dialect 130 years earlier, while Ješina 1882 for Bohemian Romani and Bodnárová 2015 for Vend Romani report the same penultimate tendency across Central Romani.

PhD dissertation, Univerzita Karlova, Filozofická fakulta, Praha. xix+478 pp. Open repository copy: CUNI DSpace hdl 20.500.11956/87448. Corroborating: Bodnárová, Zuzana. 2015. PhD dissertation, Univerzita Karlova v Praze, §3.3 Stress, pp. 108-109 (hdl 20.500.11956/80644).
catalog_quote: Proto-Romani had a grammatical and predominantly ultimate stress pattern, which is still found in various Romani dialects (Boretzky and Igla 1993: 28–34; Matras 2002: 62–63; Oslon 2012). Eastern Uzh Romani, like other Central dialects, has largely abandoned the conservative stress pattern and replaced it with fixed penultimate stress (the second-last syllable is stressed), which is typical of Polish and East Slovak dialects, e.g. čháve [ˈt͡ʃʰa.ve] ‘boys.NOM’, čháven [ˈt͡ʃʰa.ven] ‘boys.ACC’, čhavénca [t͡ʃʰa.ˈven.t͡sa] ‘with boys’, nasválo [nas.ˈva.lo] ‘ill’, nasvaľárel [nas.va.ˈʎa.rel] ‘s/he makes ill, infects’, vocative forms phéňe [ˈphe.ɲe] ‘sister’, pheňále [phe.ˈɲa.le] ‘sisters’, verb forms denášel [de.ˈna.ʃel] ‘s/he runs, flees’, dénaš [ˈde.naʃ] ‘Run away! Get away!’ (IMP.2SG), denašľáhas [de.naʃ.ˈʎa.has] ‘s/he would have run’ ... Stress is independent of the length, at least with respect to /ā/, as in šúkār [ˈʃu.kaːr] ‘beautiful’, NOM bā́ro [ˈbaː.ro] ‘big, adult’ versus DAT bāréske [baː.ˈres.ke] ‘to the big one, to the adult’, NOM jā́kha [ˈjaː.kha] ‘eyes’ versus INST jākhénca [jaː.ˈkhen.t͡sa] ‘with eyes’, and is also independent of the diphthong-like segments of mid and close vowels ... However, the lengthened mid vowels /ē/ and /ō/ (see 2.2.2.5) tend to be shortened in unstressed syllables ... Elsewhere in this dissertation, stress is only marked in borrowed East Slavic forms in which it differs from the penultimate pattern.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is fixed on the penultimate syllable of the phonological word (host plus proclitic article/preposition/te/na), regardless of vowel length; it moves with suffixation (čháve, čhavénca).
new_statements.exceptions: Antepenultimate stress in genitives with -ker-/-ger- (léskero, phraléskeri) because Layer II case suffixes are never stressed; final stress on nominative demonstratives/deictics ((k)adā́, (k)odā́, akā́, (k)ajsó, sometimes adé, ajcí) and on contracted 1SG future/imperfect forms (kerā́, kerā́s); obligatory initial stress on sávoro/sávore in all case forms and on words with the stressed negative prefixes ňi-, na- (ňíkaha, námišto, nášukār); unintegrated East Slavic loans, adverbs and particles may keep source stress (ózero, tumán, piškóm), integrated loans mostly adapt (táksis) though feminine -a loans often keep it (hosťíňica, simjá); proclitics are stressed when the host is monosyllabic (é daj, andró kher, té len, ná xal).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word including proclitic function words (article, prepositions, complementiser te, negator na), explicitly stated p. 53 and p. 318; examples are citation forms with IPA. Bodnárová 2015: 108-109 (Vend/South Central, saved file) independently gives a penultimate tendency with oblique-suffix stress and contraction-derived final stress; Ješina 1882: 4 (Bohemian) 'přízvuk je obyčejně na předposlední slabice'.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement describes Eastern Uzh Romani (Transcarpathian Ukraine: Uzhhorod district), a North Central Romani variety closest to Glottolog's East Slovakian Romani (east2314, under nort3324 North Central Romani); Beníšek states the penultimate pattern is shared by 'all Eastern North Central dialects' (p. 57). Corroborating first-hand statement for the South Central branch: Bodnárová 2015 on Kisbajom (Vend) Romani, SW Hungary = vend1247 / west2927 Western Hungarian Vend, which she says agrees with Halwachs 1998 for Burgenland Romani (burg1246). Ješina 1882 (Bohemian/Czech Romani, bohe1241) also says 'usually penultimate'. carp1235 as a whole is a dialect group; Western North Central and Romungro varieties are not covered by the opened sources, and the earlier scan note's claim of a final-vs-penultimate isogloss within Central was not verified here (Beníšek only says Central dialects 'largely abandoned' the Proto-Romani final stress).

M. nicht, alle zweisilbigen Wörter betonen demgemäss die Anfangssilbe. […] b. Dreisilbige mit kurzer Penultima legen meist den Ton auf die Anlautsilbe. […] c. Dreisilbige mit langer (geschlossener) Penultima betonen meistens diese [pp. 43-44] […] d. Mehr als dreisilbige Wörter haben bei kurzer Penultima gewöhnlich den Hauptton auf der Anfangssilbe und den Nebenton auf der Penultima, bei langer Penultima umgekehrt. [p. 45]
new_statements.translation: In the Slovak dialect the principle of paroxytone (penultimate) stress is in conflict with the law of initial-syllable stress that has penetrated from Slovak. … a. There are no oxytones in the Slovak dialect; accordingly all disyllabic words stress the first syllable. … b. Trisyllables with a short penult mostly put the stress on the initial syllable. … c. Trisyllables with a long (closed) penult mostly stress that syllable … d. Words of more than three syllables usually have, with a short penult, the main stress on the initial syllable and the secondary stress on the penult; with a long penult the reverse.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog and Beníšek 2017 record fixed penultimate stress for Eastern Uzh Romani. Sowa 1887 describes a different subdialect of the same Glottolog language (Carpathian/North Central Romani): the West Slovak Romani of the Trenčín area in 1884-85, where initial stress under Slovak influence dominates and penultimate stress survives mainly on heavy penults, with much wavering. That is a different type (weight-sensitive initial/penult alternation, never final) from the catalog's fixed penult, but it concerns a western variety 130 years earlier, so it does not refute Beníšek's statement about Eastern Uzh; Beníšek (p. 57) himself limits the penultimate pattern to the Eastern North Central dial…
new_statements.rule_in_words: For the Romani of Trenčianske Teplice (West Slovakia, recorded 1884-85): never final. Disyllables stress the first syllable. In longer words the older penultimate principle competes with Slovak initial stress and the outcome is weight-governed: a long or closed penult takes the stress (labárdi, manúšni, dadéske), a short penult leaves the main stress on the initial syllable (kókalos, číriklo, ákanak; in 4+-syllable words with secondary stress on the penult). Sowa calls the result 'ein auffallendes Schwanken' (a striking wavering) of an otherwise fairly energetic accent, and says (p. 11) the dialect has 'nearly given up' the inherited paroxytone principle in favour of the initial-stress principle of the surrounding language, unlike the Czech Romani dialect which keeps penultimate stress more purely.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Explicit: words of more than three syllables have main stress on the initial syllable and secondary stress on the penult when the penult is short, the reverse when the penult is long (p. 45, d.); the verb stem-forming suffixes in, ār, sometimes er carry a secondary stress in 4+-syllable present and perfect forms regardless of position (zákāntrínau); after a stressed negation ná/má, trisyllabic futures get a secondary stress on the penult (ná phenáva vs phénava, p. 45-46).
new_statements.exceptions: Many: some trisyllables with short penult are consistently paroxytone (manúša, kapál'i, apróha, pišálo, loans šogóris, chodníkos, večéra; all loans in -aris, e.g. mináris, zahradáris); oblique cases of feminine nouns; trisyllabic preterites in -inom/-ad'om 'quite arbitrary' but usually proparoxytone; potentials paroxytone; futures ačava/keraha proparoxytone; genitives in -eskero/-engero antepenult (čāvéskero); pronominal amenge/tumenge proparoxytone; possessives amaro/tumāro paroxytone; diminutives in -oro either stressed on the long suffix vowel (čavō'ro) or, more usually, proparoxytone with shortened o (čā'voro); adjectives in -alo likewise (bokhā'lo ~ bókhalo); many Slovak loans keep initial stress (óhlāški); atar/otar/katar heard with level stress on both syllables; the negation na/ma immediately before the verb always takes the main stress (ná darau, má phen); monosyllabic nouns throw their stress onto the article before a stressed syllable (ó rom gēlas); té stressed before monosyllabic verbs; compounds thard'ímol, čumídau stressed as single words.
new_statements.identity_note: The catalog item is named for Eastern Uzh Romani (Transcarpathia, Ukraine; Beníšek 2017), an Eastern North Central variety. Von Sowa 1887 describes the 'Mundart der slovakischen Zigeuner' recorded from speakers in Trencsén-Teplicz (Trenčianske Teplice, West Slovakia) in 1884-85, a Western North Central variety of the same Glottolog language carp1235; Sowa contrasts it with the 'cz. D.' (Czech/Moravian Romani, per Ješina 1882, which keeps penultimate stress) and the 'mg. D.' (Hungarian Romani, consistently initial). His reading applies to that western variety, not to Eastern Uzh.

Matras speaks of East Slovak Romani generally, not of t…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Matras treats the Northern Central group under 'Eastern Slovak Romani' (Eastern Uzh is not named; index has no Uzh/Transcarpathia entry): central-European Romani dialects, in contact with initial/penultimate-stress languages, have shifted stress from the inherited final (grammatical) position toward early positions; some Central dialects show consistent initial stress, whereas East Slovak Romani has the shift toward penultimate stress but keeps the conservative grammatical stress on a Layer I ending when a Layer II ending follows, so genitives like roméskero 'of the man' are stressed on the antepenult rather than the penult.
new_statements.exceptions: Layer I + Layer II case forms (e.g. roméskero) keep stress on the Layer I ending = antepenultimate, exempt from the penultimate shift; 'some Central dialects' have consistent initial stress instead; the process is described as a tendency/shift with variation in the affected groups.
new_statements.identity_note: Matras 2002 discusses 'Eastern Slovak Romani' / the Northern Central group as a whole (index: East Slovak 8, 64, 65.; Northern Central 8, 49, 51-53, 61; no entry for Uzh, Uzhhorod or Transcarpathia); the catalog language is Eastern Uzh Romani (Transcarpathian Ukraine), a North Central variety closely related to East Slovak Romani, described directly only by Beníšek 2017.

readall_conflicts: One real disagreement, explained by dialect and date: the catalog record (Beníšek 2017, §2.3 p. 52) gives fixed penultimate stress for Eastern Uzh Romani and says (p. 57) that this pattern is shared by all Eastern North Central dialects under Polish/East Slovak contact. Von Sowa 1887 (§21, pp. 41-46), describing the West Slovak Romani of Trenčianske Teplice in 1884-85, reports the opposite drift: the inherited paroxytone principle is 'in conflict' with and 'nearly given up' before the Slovak initial-stress law, so disyllables are initial-stressed, trisyllables with a short penult are mostly initial-stressed, trisyllables and longer words with a long/closed penult are mostly penult-stressed, and there are many arbitrary or lexically fixed cases; oxytones do not exist. So within Glottolog carp1235 the eastern varieties are fixed: penultimate syllable and the 19th-century western variety is weight-sensitive initial/penult; the catalog entry is explicitly for Eastern Uzh, so fixed: penultimate syllable stands for it, but a language-level entry for 'Carpathian Romani' would be heterogeneous. Matras 2002 could not be read (abstract card only), so its pp. 62-63 (cited by Beníšek for the conservative ultimate Proto-Romani pattern) add nothing here.

sources.note: §3.3 Stress, pp. 108-109: 'The stress pattern of KR [Kisbajom Romani] agrees to a great extent with that described in Halwachs (1998b: 26-29) for Burgenland Romani, according to which the stress tends to fall on the penultimate syllable of polysyllabic words.' Penult in most adjectives, NOM/ACC nouns, most verb forms; oblique cases stress the oblique suffix (antepenult in genitive daděskero); final stress from contraction (márá 'I will beat', adá, odá, asó, šukár, amen, tumen); unadapted Hungarian loans keep Hungarian initial stress; long vowels independent of stress (p. 97).
